title: Project Finance: Lending Against the Project, Not the Person
summary: In project finance the lender looks to the project's own cash flow for repayment, not to the sponsor's balance sheet. That shift changes everything: the vehicle, the recourse, the controls and who else sits at the table. Learn the frame and you understand why the documents are thick and the lender is watchful.
body:
Project finance is lending against a single project's future cash flow, held inside its own company, with the sponsor's other assets mostly out of reach. The price of that protection is control: the lender watches the project far more closely than any corporate lender would.

Recall

Q. In a condo project, what is a pre-sale threshold?

A. A minimum level of binding unit sales, usually stated as a share of units or of projected revenue, that a construction lender requires before it will fund. It is commercial practice, set loan by loan, not a statute.

Q. What does the in-balance test require at each construction draw?

A. That the undisbursed loan plus any equity still to come covers the full cost to complete. If it does not, the borrower deposits the shortfall before the lender advances again.

Q. What is residual land value?

A. What a site is worth once you take the finished value of the best permitted scheme and subtract every cost of producing it, including the developer's required profit. The land is what is left over.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the larger your projects become, the less any lender will be able to rely on you personally. A bank can size a loan on your guarantee when the loan is small next to your net worth. When the project is ten times your net worth, your guarantee is a gesture, and the lender must look somewhere else for comfort. That somewhere else is the project itself. Project finance is the discipline of making a project bankable on its own legs. If you want to build at scale, in markets where development finance institutions lend, or with partners who refuse to sign personal guarantees, you will need to speak this language.

The ring-fence: the special purpose vehicle

In plain English: you put the project in its own box, and the lender lends to the box.

The professional framing is the special purpose vehicle (SPV): a company formed to own one project and do nothing else. It holds the land, signs the construction contract, employs or contracts the operator, earns the revenue and borrows the debt. Its constitution and the loan agreement together forbid it from taking on other business, other debt or other risks. Lenders call this being bankruptcy-remote: the SPV is designed so that the troubles of its owners do not reach it, and its troubles do not reach them beyond the equity they put in.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A sponsor owns three buildings and wants to build a fourth costing 40,000,000 dollars. If the sponsor borrows in its own name, the lender can claim against all four buildings and everything else the sponsor owns. If instead the sponsor forms an SPV, contributes 16,000,000 dollars of equity and the SPV borrows 24,000,000 dollars, the lender's claim is against the SPV's assets: the fourth building, its contracts and its bank accounts. If the fourth building fails, the sponsor loses its 16,000,000 dollars of equity, and its first three buildings stay out of the fight. That is the bargain. The ring-fence works only if it is real: separate bank accounts, separate books, its own minute book and decisions recorded as the SPV's decisions, never commingled with the sponsor's.

The recourse spectrum

In plain English: recourse is how far the lender can reach past the project into your pocket, and it is not a yes-or-no question.

Picture a line. At one end is full recourse: the borrower and its guarantors owe the whole debt from everything they own. At the other is pure non-recourse: the lender may take only the project, and if the project is worth less than the debt, the lender takes the loss. Almost every real deal sits between the two, and lenders call that middle ground limited recourse. The sponsor typically supports the project fully during construction, when the risk is highest, through completion guarantees, cost-overrun support and an equity commitment. Once the project passes a defined completion test, usually physical completion plus a period of proven cash flow, that support falls away and the loan becomes non-recourse except for carve-outs for bad acts such as fraud, misapplied funds or an unauthorised transfer. These shapes are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A lender advances 24,000,000 dollars. During construction, the sponsor guarantees completion and overruns up to 4,000,000 dollars. The completion test requires the building to be finished, the occupancy certificate issued and debt service covered at least 1.30 times for two consecutive quarters. In month 30 the test is met. The 4,000,000 dollar support is released. From then on, if rents collapse, the lender's remedy is the building. The sponsor's exposure has moved from 16,000,000 dollars of equity plus 4,000,000 dollars of support to 16,000,000 dollars of equity alone.

Say that out loud now.

Full support until the completion test is met, then the project stands on its own cash flow.

Who else lends: development finance institutions and their standards

In markets where commercial banks will not lend long, a third kind of lender appears: the development finance institution (DFI). A DFI is a lender owned by one or more governments, with a mandate to finance private investment that advances development goals. The International Finance Corporation, part of the World Bank Group, is the best known, and the regional development banks have private-sector arms that lend in their regions. DFIs often lend for longer terms than commercial banks, and their presence can bring commercial lenders in alongside them.

They bring conditions. A DFI requires the project to meet its environmental and social standards: how labour is treated on site, how health and safety is managed, how community impacts, pollution and biodiversity are handled, and how affected people can complain and be heard. Many commercial banks apply a parallel framework, the Equator Principles, to their project lending. The requirements become an action plan attached to the loan, and breaching it can be an event of default. Verify the current edition of any standard against the primary source before you rely on it.

Where the project is commercially marginal but useful, DFIs and donors sometimes combine concessional money, priced below market, with commercial debt. That combination is called blended finance: the cheap layer absorbs risk or lowers the blended cost enough that commercial lenders will join. It is a tool, not a gift, and it comes with reporting.

Lender controls: the price of non-recourse

Because the lender cannot reach your other assets, it controls the project's money. Revenue goes into accounts the lender holds security over, and leaves in a fixed order: operating costs, then debt service, then reserves, and only then distributions to you. A debt service reserve account holds several months of debt service in cash. Distributions are blocked if coverage falls below a stated level. The lender takes security over the SPV's shares, contracts and accounts, and signs agreements with the contractor and operator that let it step in if the SPV defaults. Day 4 reads those documents in detail.

How the best do it

The most capable sponsors of large infrastructure and real estate projects treat bankability as a design input, not a financing afterthought. Before they commit to a contractor or an operator, they ask how a lender will see that counterparty, they allocate each risk to the party best able to carry it, and they write the contracts so the risks pass through the SPV cleanly rather than stopping inside it. A small developer can copy this with one page: list every major risk, name who carries it in the contracts, and ask whether a lender reading those contracts would agree.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: whether the SPV is taxed itself or flows through to its owners, and how its interest is deducted, depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the ring-fence limits your loss to equity plus agreed support, but only if you keep the SPV genuinely separate. Banking: expect the lender to control the accounts and the order of payments. Governance: the SPV needs its own board decisions and signing authorities, recorded as its own. Estate: SPV shares are a distinct asset that your estate plan must name, along with any support you gave. Exit: a clean, bankable SPV is easier to sell or refinance as a unit.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the SPV constitution and the loan documents; tax adviser, on the SPV's tax character.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a ring-fence that exists only on paper: shared bank accounts, the sponsor paying SPV bills from its own funds, decisions taken by the sponsor without SPV resolutions. When trouble comes, a court or a creditor may treat the SPV and the sponsor as one. The control is strict separation from day one: own accounts, own books, own minutes, and every intercompany payment documented.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "non-recourse" and assumes his personal exposure is zero. It never is. During construction he is usually guaranteeing completion, and for the life of the loan he is exposed through carve-outs. Read the recourse provisions before the interest rate.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught that the choice of vehicle, the minute book and signing authority are load-bearing, not paperwork. Project finance is where that lesson pays. The SPV's separateness is the lender's whole case for lending without your guarantee, and the minute book is the evidence that the separateness is real.

Recap

Project finance lends to a single-purpose company against the project's own cash flow. Recourse sits on a spectrum, usually full support during construction and non-recourse after a completion test, with carve-outs throughout. DFIs lend longer but bring environmental and social standards, and the lender controls the project's money in exchange for not reaching yours.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the collapse of Carillion and what it did to the projects that depended on it.
checklist: I can explain why the lender looks to the project's cash flow rather than my balance sheet.
My SPV has its own bank accounts, books, minute book and signing authorities.
I have mapped where my deal sits on the recourse spectrum, stage by stage.
I know the completion test that releases my construction support, word for word.
I have listed every carve-out that could restore personal recourse.
If a DFI is lending, I have read its environmental and social requirements before term sheet.
I know the order in which project revenue is paid out and what blocks distributions.
My estate plan names the SPV shares and any support I have signed.
head: Field checklist
speak: Project finance means the lender looks to one project's own cash flow, not to my balance sheet. The project sits in a special purpose vehicle, a company that owns that project and nothing else, so its troubles stay inside it and mine stay outside it. Recourse is a spectrum. Usually I give full support during construction, completion and cost overruns, and once the project passes a defined completion test, that support falls away and the loan becomes non-recourse except for carve-outs for bad acts such as fraud or misapplied funds. In markets where banks will not lend long, development finance institutions may lend, but they require the project to meet environmental and social standards written into the loan. Because the lender cannot reach my other assets, it controls the project's money: accounts it holds security over, a fixed order of payments, reserves, and the right to step in. My job is to keep the ring-fence real and to read the recourse terms before the rate.
terms: Special purpose vehicle (SPV) — a company formed to own and operate a single project and nothing else, so its risks are ring-fenced from its owners.
Limited recourse — a loan where the lender can reach the sponsor only in defined circumstances, typically construction support and carve-outs, and otherwise only the project.
Development finance institution (DFI) — a government-owned lender that finances private projects to advance development goals, usually with environmental and social conditions.

hostile.q: You call this non-recourse, but your SPV has no other business and no history. Why should I lend 24,000,000 dollars to a company that did not exist six months ago?
hostile.a: Because you are not lending to the company's history, you are lending to the project's cash flow, and you will control it. During construction I am supporting completion and overruns up to an agreed cap, so the risk of an unfinished building sits with me. After the completion test, you have security over the building, the contracts and the accounts, a reserve of debt service in cash, and a distribution block if coverage weakens. I will show you the contracts that pass construction and operating risk to parties strong enough to carry it.

title: Carillion: When the Contractor Inside the Ring-Fence Failed
summary: Carillion was a large British construction and services contractor that went into compulsory liquidation in January 2018, leaving public-private partnership projects part-built. The project companies were ring-fenced from their sponsors, but not from their own contractor. Roman joins Ford to show why a ring-fence is only as strong as the counterparties inside it.
rule: Rule 42: The ring-fence protects the project from its owners, not from its own counterparties; before financial close, test every key counterparty's strength as if the project's survival depended on it, and have a replacement plan you can fund.
body:
Carillion's failure in January 2018 showed that a special purpose vehicle protects a project from its sponsors' problems but not from the contractor it hired to build it. When that contractor collapsed, the project companies that relied on it were left with part-built hospitals and contracts to re-let.

Recall

Q. What is the recourse spectrum?

A. The range from full recourse, where the borrower and guarantors owe the debt from everything they own, to pure non-recourse, where the lender may take only the project. Most project loans are limited recourse in between.

Q. What does a completion guarantee usually cover?

A. The guarantor's promise that the project will be finished, often by a stated date and to a stated standard, and that the guarantor will fund what it takes to get there. Its triggers and caps are negotiated, not standard.

Q. In land acquisition, what is an option agreement?

A. A contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy land on agreed terms within a period, usually for a fee, so the buyer can complete diligence and approvals before committing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this failure lives on the lender's side of the ledger as much as the builder's. Yesterday Priya taught the ring-fence. Today we test it. A project company can be perfectly separate from its owners and still die, because it has handed its biggest risks to one outside party. If that party fails, the ring-fence keeps the problem in, which is exactly what you do not want.

The facts below are limited to what is publicly reported and widely documented. Where I describe the inside of a typical project company, I am describing the general structure, not any one project's documents.

1. Timeline

Carillion was one of the United Kingdom's largest construction and facilities services contractors, active in public-private partnership work, where a private project company finances, builds and maintains a public asset such as a hospital and is paid by the public sector over decades. In July 2017 Carillion issued a profit warning and wrote down the value of several large contracts, and its chief executive stepped down. Further warnings followed in the autumn. In January 2018, after talks with lenders and the government failed, the company entered compulsory liquidation. Two large hospital projects it was building, the Royal Liverpool University Hospital and the Midland Metropolitan Hospital, were left unfinished, and completing them took years more. In May 2018 two parliamentary committees published a joint report sharply criticising the board, the auditors and the government's oversight.

2. Key decisions

Three kinds of decision mattered. Carillion's own decisions to bid aggressively for large, fixed-price contracts with thin margins. The decisions of project companies and their lenders to accept one contractor for both construction and long-term services, concentrating risk in a single counterparty. And the public sector's decisions to keep awarding work to a contractor already issuing warnings.

3. Assumptions

The central assumption was that a contractor of that size could absorb losses on individual contracts. A second was that the contractor's security package, its bonds and parent guarantees, would cover a failure. A third, built into how many project financings are structured, was that construction risk had been passed down to the contractor and therefore off the project company's books. Passing a risk down a contract does not make it disappear. It makes it a credit risk on whoever accepted it.

4. Incentives

The contractor was rewarded for winning work and booking revenue, which favoured optimistic contract accounting. Project sponsors were rewarded for a low construction price, which favoured the aggressive bidder. Lenders were comforted by a fixed-price contract with a large name and tended to read the price rather than the contractor's balance sheet.

5. Warning signs ignored

Public reporting describes large and growing pension obligations, rising debt, reliance on extending the time it took to pay its suppliers, and the July 2017 write-down itself. After a profit warning of that scale, any project company relying on the contractor had a clear signal to test its replacement plan. A counterparty's warning is your warning.

Say that out loud now.

A risk passed down a contract becomes a credit risk on whoever accepted it.

6. Point of no return

For Carillion, the point of no return was the failure of the January 2018 rescue talks. For the project companies, it arrived earlier and more quietly: the day each one reached financial close with a single contractor whose failure it had no funded plan to survive. After that, the bonds and guarantees were whatever they were, and the cost of re-letting a half-built hospital fell where the contracts and the market put it.

7. Root cause

Roman's reading is that the root cause was concentration without a test of strength. The project structures were designed to move risk away from the public sector and the lenders, and they did, onto a contractor whose ability to carry it was assumed rather than measured. The security package was sized to a normal default, not to a total collapse of a major firm with many projects failing at once.

What it means for a developer

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. Your SPV signs a 30,000,000 dollar fixed-price contract. The contractor provides a performance bond for 10 percent, 3,000,000 dollars, a commercial convention in many markets rather than a rule. Halfway through, the contractor fails. A replacement contractor, inheriting half-finished work it did not build and will not warrant, prices the remaining 15,000,000 dollars of work at 19,000,000 dollars, plus 1,000,000 dollars of delay interest. Your gap is 5,000,000 dollars. The bond covers 3,000,000 dollars, if the surety pays promptly, which it may contest. The other 2,000,000 dollars comes from contingency, from you, or from a lender who is now deciding whether to keep funding.

A second example. Suppose, before close, you had asked what it would cost to replace the contractor at the halfway point and found the answer was 5,000,000 dollars. You could then have raised the bond, required a parent company guarantee from a stronger entity, held more contingency, or chosen a contractor whose failure was less likely. The test costs a spreadsheet and an afternoon. Skipping it cost the developer in the first example 2,000,000 dollars.

The prevention habit

Roman's prevention habit is a counterparty card for every party that carries a major risk in your project: the contractor, the operator, the main tenant, the surety and any guarantor. On one page, write what the party owes you, what it would cost to replace it at the worst moment, the security you hold against that cost, and three signals you will watch, such as its published results, its suppliers' complaints and its own lenders' actions. Review the cards quarterly and whenever news breaks. A card that shows replacement cost above security is a decision you must make now, while you still have choices, not after the warning has become a liquidation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a large contractor's name as a credit rating. The control is to read the contractor's financial statements, ask for its order book and margins, check how long it takes to pay its own suppliers, and size your security to the cost of replacing it at the worst point in the build.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that a fixed-price contract has fixed the price. It has fixed the price only for as long as the contractor survives. A fixed price from a weak contractor is an option the contractor holds, and it exercises it by failing.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Roman took a composite case in which a contractor billed ahead of the work and then failed, and the guarantees were called. Carillion is the same failure at national scale: the money and the risk had both moved to the contractor, and when it fell, they came back to whoever was left holding the project.

Recap

Carillion's collapse left ring-fenced projects part-built because their biggest risks sat with one contractor whose strength was assumed. The lesson is to test every key counterparty's ability to carry the risk you pass to it, and to fund a replacement plan before close. Rule 42 states it.

Next: Priya, on The Money: what non-recourse debt really costs, and when blended finance changes the answer.
checklist: I have read the financial statements of every key counterparty, not just its name.
I have priced the cost of replacing my contractor at the worst point in the build.
My bonds and guarantees are sized to that replacement cost, not to convention.
I know which counterparty carries each major risk and whether it can afford to.
I monitor my contractor's payment of its own suppliers during the build.
I treat a counterparty's profit warning as a trigger to test my replacement plan.
I have a named fallback contractor or a process to appoint one quickly.
I have written Rule 42 in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was a large British contractor that went into compulsory liquidation in January 2018, leaving public-private partnership hospitals part-built. The project companies were ring-fenced from their owners, but they had passed their biggest risks to one contractor, and passing a risk down a contract only turns it into a credit risk on whoever accepted it. The warning signs were public: a large profit warning in July 2017, growing obligations, slow payment of suppliers. The root cause was concentration without a test of strength. For me, the lesson is a calculation. Before financial close, I price what it would cost to replace my contractor halfway through, and I size my bonds, guarantees and contingency to that number. I read the contractor's accounts, not just its name, and I treat its warning as my warning. Rule 42: the ring-fence protects the project from its owners, not from its own counterparties.
terms: Public-private partnership — an arrangement where a private project company finances, builds and often maintains a public asset in exchange for payments over a long term.
Performance bond — a surety's promise to pay up to a stated amount if the contractor fails to perform, subject to the bond's conditions.
Counterparty risk — the risk that a party to a contract with you fails to perform or pay.

hostile.q: Your contractor is one of the biggest in the country. Why are you asking for a parent guarantee and a larger bond? Are you saying you do not trust us?
hostile.a: I am saying my lender and I have priced what it would cost to finish this building with someone else, and we need security that matches that number. Size is not the same as strength, and the largest firms have failed before. If your balance sheet is as strong as your name, the guarantee costs you little. If you would rather not give it, I will need to hold more contingency, and that changes the price I can accept.

title: What Non-Recourse Debt Really Costs
summary: Non-recourse debt protects your other assets, and you pay for that protection in margin, lower leverage, cash reserves and transaction costs. Blended finance can lower the cost of a marginal project, but only if you count every condition attached. Learn to compare the all-in cost, not the headline rate.
body:
The protection of non-recourse debt is not free. You pay for it in a higher margin, less leverage, cash locked in reserves, and heavy upfront costs, and only the all-in number tells you whether the protection is worth the price.

Recall

Q. What makes a special purpose vehicle bankruptcy-remote?

A. Its constitution and loan documents limit it to one project and forbid other business, debt or risks, so the problems of its owners do not reach it, and its problems do not reach them beyond their equity.

Q. What is a lender's monitor?

A. An independent engineer or cost consultant hired to verify progress and cost on the lender's behalf, usually at the borrower's expense.

Q. What is absorption in a feasibility study?

A. The rate at which the market takes up new supply, such as units sold or leased per month, expressed as a number tied to evidence, not an adjective.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender will show you a margin over a reference rate and call it the price. It is one line of the price. If you compare two financing offers on margin alone, you will often choose the more expensive one. Today you learn to count everything that moves money out of your pocket, or locks it up, because of the way the debt is structured.

Five costs beyond the coupon

The first cost is the margin itself. Project lenders cannot reach your other assets, so they charge more than a corporate lender would for the same project, as commercial practice. The second is lower leverage: they lend a smaller share of cost, because the project is their only source of repayment, so you put in more equity, and equity is the most expensive money you have. The third is reserves: a debt service reserve account, often several months of payments, funded in cash at close or from early cash flow, earning little and unavailable to you. The fourth is transaction cost: lenders' legal fees, their technical, insurance and market advisers, environmental and social diligence, and arrangement fees, all usually paid by the borrower. The fifth is time: project financings take months to close, and every month of delay carries land, interest and opportunity cost.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 50,000,000 dollar project. Offer A is a corporate-style loan with your full guarantee: 70 percent of cost, 35,000,000 dollars, at a 7 percent all-in rate, with modest fees. Offer B is a project loan with no guarantee after completion: 60 percent of cost, 30,000,000 dollars, at 8 percent, with a six-month debt service reserve and 1,000,000 dollars of extra transaction costs. Under B you put in 5,000,000 dollars more equity, plus the reserve, plus the extra costs. If your equity needs a 15 percent return, that extra 5,000,000 dollars alone costs you about 750,000 dollars a year in required return, before the higher interest rate. Offer B is clearly more expensive. The question is whether the protection is worth it.

Pricing the protection

In plain English: the extra cost of non-recourse debt is an insurance premium against losing everything else you own.

The professional framing is to compare the extra cost with the exposure it removes. Under Offer A, if the project fails badly, your guarantee puts your other assets behind the loan. Under Offer B, after completion, your loss is capped at your equity. If your other assets are small, the protection is worth little and A may be right. If you own several buildings and a family's security sits behind them, the protection may be worth far more than its premium. There is no universal answer, which is why this is a judgment, not a formula.

Say that out loud now.

The extra cost of non-recourse debt is a premium, and I pay it only when the exposure it removes is worth more.

Blended finance and DFI money

A development finance institution may offer something commercial lenders cannot: a longer term. A longer amortisation lowers annual debt service, which lifts debt service coverage and can increase the loan a project can carry. Blended finance adds a concessional layer, priced below market, which lowers the blended cost.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A 40,000,000 dollar loan has two tranches. A commercial tranche of 30,000,000 dollars at 9 percent and a concessional tranche of 10,000,000 dollars at 3 percent. The blended rate is the weighted average: 30 times 9 is 270, plus 10 times 3 is 30, total 300, divided by 40, which is 7.5 percent. On interest alone, the concessional layer saves 600,000 dollars a year against borrowing the whole 40,000,000 dollars at 9 percent. Now subtract the costs it brings: the environmental and social action plan, independent monitoring, impact reporting, and perhaps design changes to meet the standards. If those cost 150,000 dollars a year, the true saving is 450,000 dollars. Still worth it, but now you know the real number.

Building the comparison, in order

Priya's order of operations keeps the comparison honest. First, put every offer on the same project, the same cost and the same schedule, so you compare financing and nothing else. Second, compute the loan each offer will actually advance, using its own binding limit, not the amount the lender mentioned in the first meeting. Third, compute the equity each offer requires, including reserves and fees, which are uses of funds. Fourth, price that equity at the return your investors require, because equity that sits in a project is equity that is not earning elsewhere. Fifth, add interest at each offer's rate and the cost of each month to close. Sixth, write the exposure each offer leaves on your personal balance sheet: guarantees, carve-outs and how long each lasts.

The answer is rarely that one offer wins on every line. It is usually that one is cheaper and riskier and the other is dearer and safer, and the table forces you to choose deliberately rather than by habit. Write the choice and the reason in your decision journal. In two years, when you look back, you will want to know whether you paid for protection you needed or protection you did not.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. A personal guarantee is a contingent liability: it does not show as a debt until it is called, and then it shows all at once. A non-recourse loan inside an SPV shows on your balance sheet only as the equity you have at risk. When you add up what you own, list every guarantee beside the asset it backs, with its cap and the date it ends. A net worth that ignores guarantees is overstated. Choosing non-recourse debt is often less about the project and more about keeping your own balance sheet honest and survivable. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing offers on headline rate and discovering after close that reserves, fees and lower leverage made the cheap loan the dear one. The control is an all-in cost table for every offer: rate, leverage, equity required and its cost, reserves, fees and time to close, side by side.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats concessional money as free money. It is cheaper money with obligations, and the obligations have a cost. Price the conditions, then decide.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage warned that an internal rate of return can flatter a deal and that after-tax leakage matters. The same discipline applies to debt: the headline rate flatters the loan, and the reserves, fees and extra equity are the leakage. Count them, or the deal you approve is not the deal you get.

Recap

Non-recourse debt costs more in margin, leverage, reserves, fees and time. The extra cost is a premium against exposure of your other assets, and it is worth paying only when that exposure matters. Blended finance can lower the blended rate, but its conditions have a cost too. Compare offers all-in.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: the security package, direct agreements and step-in rights.
checklist: I compare financing offers on an all-in cost table, not the headline rate.
I price the extra equity each offer requires at my required equity return.
I include reserves, arrangement fees and lenders' adviser costs in every comparison.
I estimate time to close and its carrying cost for each offer.
I can say what exposure a non-recourse structure removes and what it is worth to me.
I price the conditions attached to any concessional money before accepting it.
My personal balance sheet lists every guarantee beside the asset it backs.
head: Field checklist
speak: Non-recourse debt protects my other assets, and I pay for that protection five ways. A higher margin, because the lender can only look to the project. Lower leverage, so I put in more equity, which is my most expensive money. Cash reserves, often several months of debt service, locked away. Transaction costs, lenders' lawyers and advisers, paid by me. And time, because project financings take months. So I never compare offers on rate alone. I build an all-in table: rate, leverage, equity needed and its cost, reserves, fees and time to close. Then I ask whether the protection is worth its premium, which depends on what else I own. Blended finance can lower the blended rate, for example a 3 percent tranche beside a 9 percent tranche, but it brings standards, monitoring and reporting, and those cost money too. A personal guarantee is a contingent liability that appears all at once when called, so my balance sheet lists every one.
terms: All-in cost — the full cost of a financing, including rate, fees, reserves, the cost of extra equity and time, not just the headline margin.
Debt service reserve account — a cash account, usually holding several months of debt service, that the lender can draw on if project cash falls short.
Blended finance — combining concessional money priced below market with commercial debt to make a marginal but useful project financeable.

hostile.q: Our project loan is priced at 8 percent against your bank's offer of 7. You say ours is worth it. Prove it.
hostile.a: On rate alone it is not. All-in, your offer needs 5,000,000 dollars more equity, a six-month reserve and about 1,000,000 dollars more in transaction costs, so it costs more. What it buys is that after completion my other assets are not behind the loan. I have valued that exposure, and for this portfolio the protection is worth more than the premium. If the numbers were the other way, I would take the bank's offer.

title: The Security Package, Direct Agreements and Step-In Rights
summary: A project lender who cannot reach your other assets takes security over everything the project owns and every contract it relies on. Direct agreements with the contractor and operator let the lender step into the project instead of watching it die. Learn how the package fits together and which clauses decide your control.
body:
The project lender's real protection is not the building alone but a web of security over the project's shares, accounts and contracts, plus direct agreements that let the lender step in and keep the project alive if you default. Read that web as carefully as the loan itself, because it decides when you lose control.

Recall

Q. Name the five costs of non-recourse debt beyond the headline rate.

A. A higher margin, lower leverage and therefore more equity, cash reserves, transaction costs paid by the borrower, and the time it takes to close.

Q. What is a carve-out in a construction loan?

A. A defined exception to limited recourse, such as fraud, misapplied funds or an unauthorised transfer, that makes the guarantor personally liable, either for the lender's loss or, if it springs, for the whole loan.

Q. What is an easement on title?

A. A right held by someone else over your land, such as a right of way or a utility corridor, that runs with the land and limits what you can build or do there.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in a corporate loan, default usually means the lender sues you. In project finance, default means the lender may take over the project company, its contracts and its cash, and run it without you. The documents that allow that are often signed late at night at closing, in a stack of forty, and many sponsors never read them. This lesson tells you which ones to read and what to fight for. I teach concepts and how to think; the enforceability of every point depends on local law, so verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

The security package

In plain English: the lender takes a claim over everything the project needs to survive, so that no one else can get to it first.

The professional framing is the security package: the full set of security interests the lender takes. Typically it includes a mortgage or charge over the land and building, a pledge over the shares of the special purpose vehicle, security over the project's bank accounts, an assignment by way of security of the project's key contracts and insurance proceeds, and security over any receivables. The share pledge matters most to you. It lets the lender, on enforcement, take the SPV itself rather than selling the building out of it, which keeps the contracts, permits and licences intact. It also means the lender can take your company without a court sale of the land, where local law allows.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. An SPV owns a 40,000,000 dollar building with 24,000,000 dollars of debt, a construction contract, an operating agreement, permits and a reserve account holding 1,500,000 dollars. On default, a lender with only a mortgage must sell the building, and a buyer may have to re-apply for permits and re-sign contracts. A lender with a share pledge can take the SPV, keep everything in place, and sell the shares as a running business. The second route preserves more value, which is why lenders insist on it, and why you must understand that the share pledge is a pledge of your ownership, not just of a building.

Direct agreements and step-in rights

In plain English: the lender signs its own side agreement with each key contractor so that, if the project company fails, the contractor keeps working for the lender instead of walking away.

The professional framing is the direct agreement, sometimes called a tripartite agreement or a consent agreement: a contract among the lender, the project company and a key counterparty such as the construction contractor or operator. Its core terms are three. First, the counterparty must notify the lender before terminating its contract for the project company's default, and must give the lender a period to cure. Second, the lender gains step-in rights: the right to take over the project company's position in the contract, directly or through a nominee, for a period. Third, the lender may novate the contract, that is, transfer it to a new owner of the project, so the buyer inherits a working contract.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The SPV misses two payments to its contractor. Without a direct agreement, the contract may let the contractor terminate, demobilise and leave a half-built frame. With one, the contractor must first notify the lender and wait, say 45 days, during which the lender can pay the arrears and step in. The building keeps rising. The notice period and the length of the step-in are negotiated, and they are the clauses to read first.

Say that out loud now.

Notice to the lender, time to cure, the right to step in, and the right to pass the contract on.

Covenants that come from standards

When a development finance institution or an Equator Principles bank lends, its environmental and social requirements are written into the loan as covenants and conditions. Usually there is an environmental and social action plan with dated actions, a duty to report incidents, a duty to keep a grievance mechanism through which affected people can raise complaints, and the lender's right to appoint an independent monitor. Breach of the plan can be an event of default. DFIs also apply sanctions and integrity rules: a sponsor found to have engaged in corrupt or fraudulent practice can be barred from future financing. Verify the current edition of any standard and the exact loan wording against the primary source before you rely on them.

The accounts agreement

One more document deserves a sponsor's attention: the accounts agreement, which sets out the project's bank accounts and the order in which money moves between them. Revenue lands in a proceeds account and is swept into an operating account, a debt service account, the reserve accounts and, last, a distribution account. Each transfer has conditions. If coverage falls below a stated level, money that would have reached the distribution account is trapped and held, or used to prepay debt. In plain English, the accounts agreement is the plumbing that turns the lender's controls into daily practice. Read which events trap cash, who may instruct the bank, and how quickly trapped cash is released once the problem is cured.

What to read and what to negotiate

Five points deserve your attention before you sign. The events that let the lender enforce the share pledge, and whether there is a cure period. The length of the cure and step-in periods in each direct agreement. Whether the lender may step in for minor defaults or only for serious ones. Whether, after step-in, the lender is liable for the project company's past debts to the counterparty; lenders usually refuse, and counterparties push back. And whether environmental and social breaches have their own cure periods, since an incident on site is not the same as a missed payment.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's counsel on the security package and every direct agreement; environmental and social specialist, on the action plan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a share pledge that can be enforced on a technical default without a cure period, so a missed report becomes a lost company. The control is a cure-period matrix: every default, its notice requirement and its cure time, negotiated before close and kept on file for the life of the loan.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks direct agreements are the lender's business and the contractor's business, not his. They decide how fast he can lose the project and who can finish it, so they are his business more than anyone's.

Callback

In Week 30, LEX taught title: ownership forms, encumbrances and what runs with the land. The security package is title thinking extended to the whole project. The lender takes an encumbrance over the land, and over the company that owns the land, and over the contracts that make the land worth something.

Recap

The security package covers the land, the SPV's shares, its accounts, its contracts and its insurance. Direct agreements give the lender notice, cure, step-in and novation rights with key counterparties. Environmental and social standards arrive as covenants. Negotiate cure periods before close, because they decide how quickly you can lose the project.

Next: Priya, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a project loan from the coverage covenant back to the equity you must raise.
checklist: I have listed every element of the security package and what each one reaches.
I understand that the share pledge is a pledge of my ownership of the SPV.
I know the events that allow the lender to enforce the share pledge.
I have read the notice, cure and step-in periods in every direct agreement.
I know whether a stepping-in lender is liable for the SPV's past debts.
I have a cure-period matrix for every event of default.
I have read the environmental and social action plan and its reporting duties.
My lawyer has signed off on the security package and direct agreements.
head: Field checklist
speak: A project lender cannot reach my other assets, so it takes security over everything the project needs to survive: a mortgage over the land and building, a pledge over the shares of the special purpose vehicle, security over the bank accounts, and an assignment of the key contracts and insurance. The share pledge matters most to me, because it lets the lender take my company itself and keep the permits and contracts intact. Then come direct agreements with the contractor and the operator. They require the counterparty to notify the lender before terminating, give the lender time to cure, allow the lender to step into the contract, and let it pass the contract to a new owner. If a development finance institution lends, its environmental and social standards become covenants, and a breach can be a default. Before I sign, I build a matrix of every default, its notice and its cure period, because those periods decide how fast I can lose the project.
terms: Security package — the full set of security interests a lender takes over a project's land, shares, accounts, contracts and insurance.
Direct agreement — a contract among the lender, the project company and a key counterparty, giving the lender notice, cure and step-in rights.
Step-in rights — the lender's right to take over the project company's position in a key contract for a period after a default.

hostile.q: We will not give your lender 90 days to cure before we can terminate. If you stop paying us, we stop working. Why should we finance your default?
hostile.a: You are not financing it. During the cure period the lender will either pay the arrears or step in and pay you going forward, and the agreement will say so. What the period buys is time for a solvent party to keep you working instead of leaving a half-built frame that no one can finish. I can accept a shorter period for payment defaults than for other defaults. Let us agree the number and a clear payment obligation on step-in.

title: Reverse Engineering a Project Loan From the Coverage Covenant
summary: A project lender sizes the loan backward from cash flow: the debt service the project can carry, then the loan that payment supports. Start from a finished term sheet and work backward to the loan amount, the binding limit and the equity you must raise. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
A project lender does not ask how much you want to borrow. It asks how much debt service the project's cash can carry, then works out what loan that payment supports. Run that calculation yourself, backward from the term sheet, and you know the loan before the lender tells you.

Recall

Q. What three things does a direct agreement give a lender?

A. Notice before a key counterparty terminates for the project company's default, a period to cure, and the right to step in and, if needed, pass the contract to a new owner.

Q. What is an interest reserve in a construction loan?

A. A line within the loan budget set aside to pay interest as it falls due during construction, when the project has no income. It is borrowed money, so it is itself charged interest.

Q. What does a highest and best use analysis test?

A. Which use of a site is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and, among those, maximally productive.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender's term sheet states a coverage covenant, a term, a rate and a cap on loan to cost. Most sponsors read those and wait for the lender's sizing. You will reverse engineer: start from the finished terms and work backward to the loan, find which limit binds, and know your equity gap the same day. All numbers are hypothetical round figures.

The finished term sheet

A development finance institution offers a project loan on these terms. Minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), meaning stabilised net operating income (NOI) divided by annual debt service, of 1.30. Fifteen-year amortisation with level annual payments. An interest rate of 8 percent. Maximum loan to cost of 60 percent. A debt service reserve account holding six months of debt service, funded at close. The project costs 50,000,000 dollars and the stabilised NOI in your pro forma is 4,000,000 dollars a year.

Step 1: the debt service the project can carry

Work backward from coverage. If NOI divided by debt service must be at least 1.30, then debt service can be at most NOI divided by 1.30. 4,000,000 dollars divided by 1.30 is about 3,077,000 dollars a year. That is the ceiling on what the project may pay the lender.

Step 2: the loan that payment supports

A level payment that repays a loan over a fixed term is set by an annuity factor: the share of the original loan paid each year. For 8 percent over 15 years the factor is about 0.1168, which means each year's payment is about 11.68 percent of the original loan. Work backward: loan equals debt service divided by the factor. 3,077,000 dollars divided by 0.1168 is about 26,340,000 dollars. That is the maximum loan coverage allows.

Say that out loud now.

NOI over coverage gives the payment; payment over the annuity factor gives the loan.

Step 3: the other limit, and which one binds

Loan to cost caps the loan at 60 percent of 50,000,000 dollars, which is 30,000,000 dollars. The lender will lend the smaller of the two: 26,340,000 dollars. Coverage binds. This is the sizing to the binding limit you learned in Week 36. Notice what it tells you: the project's income, not its cost, is the constraint. Spending more on construction will not raise the loan; raising NOI would.

Step 4: the equity gap, including the reserve

The reserve must hold six months of debt service: half of 3,077,000 dollars, about 1,540,000 dollars, in cash at close. That cash is a use of funds. Total uses are 50,000,000 dollars of project cost plus 1,540,000 dollars of reserve, 51,540,000 dollars. The loan supplies 26,340,000 dollars. Equity must supply the rest: about 25,200,000 dollars. On a project you may have pictured as 60 percent debt, you are raising roughly 49 percent of uses as equity.

Step 5: what NOI would unlock the full 30,000,000 dollars?

Keep reversing. To borrow the full 30,000,000 dollars, debt service would be 30,000,000 times 0.1168, about 3,505,000 dollars. Coverage of 1.30 then requires NOI of 3,505,000 times 1.30, about 4,560,000 dollars. Your pro forma shows 4,000,000 dollars, so you are 560,000 dollars a year short, or 14 percent. That is a precise question for your market team: is there honest evidence for 14 percent more income, through rent, occupancy or lower operating cost? If there is not, do not invent it; raise the equity.

Step 6: what a longer term does

A DFI's chief advantage is often tenor. Suppose the same lender offered 20-year amortisation at 8 percent. The annuity factor falls to about 0.1019. The same 3,077,000 dollars of debt service now supports about 30,200,000 dollars, so the 60 percent loan-to-cost cap of 30,000,000 dollars binds instead, and equity falls by about 3,660,000 dollars. Five more years of term raised the loan by more than any plausible rent increase. This is why sponsors in long-tenor markets fight for term before rate.

The table

Item15-year term20-year term
Maximum debt service3,077,0003,077,000
Loan by coverage26,340,00030,200,000
Loan by loan to cost30,000,00030,000,000
Loan offered26,340,00030,000,000
Binding limitCoverageLoan to cost

All figures are hypothetical, in dollars. Coverage levels, terms and caps are commercial practice, not standards; verify every figure against your own term sheet.

Step 7: check the answer forward

A reverse calculation is only trustworthy once you have run it forward again. Take the 26,340,000 dollar loan. Multiply by the annuity factor of 0.1168: debt service is about 3,077,000 dollars. Divide NOI of 4,000,000 dollars by that payment: coverage is 1.30, exactly the covenant. Divide the loan by cost: 26,340,000 over 50,000,000 is about 53 percent, under the 60 percent cap. Add loan and equity: 26,340,000 plus 25,200,000 is 51,540,000, matching total uses. Every check closes, so the reverse was right. Do this every time; a single slip in the annuity factor moves the loan by millions.

What you say to the lender

With these numbers you can open the next call with a sentence rather than a question. "On your terms, coverage binds at about 26,300,000 dollars, so we are raising about 25,200,000 of equity including the reserve. We would like to discuss a 20-year amortisation, which on our numbers lets loan to cost bind at 30,000,000 instead." The lender now knows you have done the work, and the conversation moves to tenor, which is where the value is.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing the loan on an optimistic NOI, closing, and then failing the coverage covenant in year one, which blocks distributions or triggers default. The control is to size your own expectations on a conservative NOI and to see how far income can fall before coverage breaks, which Roman takes further in Week 44.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets that the reserve is a use of funds. He raises equity for the cost and finds at closing that the lender wants another 1,540,000 dollars in a reserve account before it advances a dollar.

A second beginner's mistake is to use an interest-only payment in the sizing. Interest alone on 26,340,000 dollars at 8 percent is about 2,107,000 dollars a year, which flatters coverage to about 1.90. The lender sizes on the full level payment, principal and interest, and so must you. If the loan has an interest-only period at the start, size coverage on the amortising payment that follows, because that is the payment the project must eventually carry.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught debt service coverage, debt yield and sizing to the binding limit. Today you ran the same logic backward from a term sheet, and saw that in project finance coverage often binds, and that tenor can matter more than rate.

Recap

Divide NOI by the coverage ratio to find the maximum debt service; divide that by the annuity factor to find the loan. Compare with loan to cost and take the smaller. Add the reserve to uses before you size equity. Then reverse once more to find the NOI that would unlock more debt, and test whether a longer term matters more than a lower rate.

Next: Priya, on The Room: the development finance institution's appraisal visit and the environmental and social questions.
checklist: I can compute maximum debt service as NOI divided by the coverage ratio.
I can convert debt service to a loan amount using the annuity factor.
I compare the coverage limit with loan to cost and identify the binding limit.
I add the debt service reserve to uses before sizing equity.
I can work out the NOI needed to unlock a larger loan.
I test how a longer term changes the loan before negotiating rate.
My sizing uses a conservative NOI, not the most hopeful one.
head: Field checklist
speak: A project lender sizes the loan backward from cash flow, so I do the same. Start with stabilised net operating income, say 4,000,000 dollars. Divide by the minimum coverage ratio of 1.30, and the project can carry about 3,077,000 dollars of debt service a year. Divide that by the annuity factor, about 0.1168 for 8 percent over 15 years, and the loan is about 26,340,000 dollars. Loan to cost at 60 percent of 50,000,000 dollars would allow 30,000,000, so coverage binds and the lender offers the smaller figure. Then I add the six-month reserve, about 1,540,000 dollars, to uses, and raise about 25,200,000 dollars of equity. Reversing once more, I would need about 4,560,000 dollars of NOI to borrow the full 30,000,000 dollars, 14 percent more income than I can honestly show. And a 20-year term would lift the loan to the cap without any rent increase, so I fight for tenor first.
terms: Annuity factor — the share of an original loan paid each year under level payments that fully repay it over the term at a given rate.
Binding limit — the sizing test, such as coverage or loan to cost, that produces the smallest loan and therefore sets the amount offered.
Tenor — the length of time over which a loan is repaid.

hostile.q: Your model assumes 4,000,000 dollars of stabilised NOI. If it comes in at 3,600,000, what happens to coverage on the loan you want?
hostile.a: On the 26,340,000 dollar loan, debt service is about 3,077,000 dollars, so 3,600,000 of NOI gives coverage of about 1.17, below the 1.30 covenant. Distributions would be blocked and, depending on the wording, we could be near a default. That is why I have sized our expectations to the lower loan, funded the reserve, and stress-tested income. I would rather borrow less now than breach in year one.

title: The Appraisal Visit: Answering the Environmental and Social Questions
summary: A development finance institution's appraisal team visits the site and asks about labour, safety, community impact and complaints. They are not testing your goodwill; they are testing whether you have a system. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say and the question behind each question.
body:
When a development finance institution's appraisal team asks about workers' housing, safety and complaints from neighbours, it is not asking whether you are a good person. It is asking whether you run a system that will still work when you are not watching, and your answers are the evidence.

Recall

Q. How do you find the maximum loan from a coverage covenant?

A. Divide net operating income by the minimum coverage ratio to get the maximum annual debt service, then divide that by the annuity factor for the rate and term.

Q. In a condo project, why are buyers' deposits usually held in trust or escrow?

A. To protect buyers if the project fails, so their money is not available to the developer's general creditors. The rules on when deposits may be used vary by jurisdiction.

Q. What is the purpose of a non-disclosure agreement in land acquisition?

A. To protect confidential information exchanged during negotiation and diligence, such as price, plans and reports, and to limit how either side may use it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a DFI loan can give you a tenor no commercial bank offers, but the appraisal is where it is won or lost. Sponsors lose these meetings not because their projects are harmful but because they answer standards questions with reassurance instead of evidence. The appraisal team writes a report for its credit committee, and every vague sentence becomes a condition, a delay or a declined loan.

The scene

A hypothetical 300-unit residential project, three months from financial close. Two people from the DFI arrive: an investment officer and an environmental and social specialist. Your construction manager and your community liaison are with you. After the site walk, in the site office, the specialist opens a notebook and asks: "Tell me about the workers. Where do they sleep, who pays them, and what happens when one is hurt?"

The question behind the question

The surface question is about labour. The real questions are three. Does the sponsor know, or will he have to ask? Does the obligation reach the subcontractors, where most workers are employed? And is there a record that proves it? A specialist has seen many projects where the main contractor's policies are excellent and the subcontractors' workers have none of them.

The lines to say

Start with the system. "There are about 180 workers on site at peak, roughly three-quarters employed by subcontractors. Every subcontract carries the same labour and safety clauses as the main contract, and our construction manager audits a sample of subcontractor payroll each month. Here is last month's audit."

Then the incident record. "We record every incident and near miss in one log. In the last quarter we had two lost-time injuries, both investigated within 48 hours. Here are the reports and the corrective actions."

Then the community. "Neighbours can raise a complaint by phone, in writing or in person at the site gate. Each complaint is logged, acknowledged within a set time and closed with a written response. Our liaison will walk you through the open items."

Then the gap, honestly. "Our weakest area is dust on the access road in the dry season. We have a watering schedule, but complaints show it is not enough. We propose adding a wheel wash and paving the first section before the next dry season, and we would like that as a dated action in the plan."

Say that out loud now.

Here is the system, here is the record, here is the gap and the date we close it.

The lines never to say

Never say "that is the contractor's responsibility." The DFI lends to you, and it holds you to the standard across the site. Never say "we have never had a complaint." The specialist will hear either that you have no way to receive complaints or that you are not telling the truth. Never say "we comply with all local laws" as if that were the end of the matter; DFI standards can go further than local law, and saying this suggests you have not read them. Never promise an action you have not priced; an action plan item becomes a loan covenant.

When to stay silent

When the specialist is writing, stop talking. Notes are being taken for a report, and a second explanation sounds like doubt about the first. When your community liaison is answering a question about a complaint, let the liaison finish, even if you would phrase it better. The team is testing whether your staff own the system.

Holding your state

Standards questions can feel like accusations. They are not. Breathe slowly between answers, and treat each question as a request for a document. If you feel defensive, ask yourself what record would answer the question, and offer to send it.

Worked examples: two answers to the same question

The specialist asks: "What happens if a neighbour's house cracks during piling?" Weak answer: "That will not happen; our engineer is very good." Strong answer: "Before piling we commissioned a pre-condition survey of the 12 nearest buildings, with photographs, shared with the owners. We monitor vibration at three points during piling, with a stop level set by our geotechnical engineer. If a neighbour reports damage, it goes through the grievance log, and our insurer and engineer assess it against the survey." The second answer costs perhaps 20,000 dollars of surveys and monitors. It is the answer that gets the loan.

A second example. The officer asks: "Who on your side signs the quarterly environmental and social report?" Weak: "Our consultant prepares it." Strong: "Our consultant prepares it; I review and sign it as a director of the SPV, and it goes to the board with the financial report." The DFI wants a named accountable person, not a consultant.

Closing the meeting

End by summarising what you heard, not what you said. "I have three items from today: the dust controls on the access road, the second audit of the scaffolding subcontractor, and the timing of the community meeting before piling. I will send a priced update of the action plan covering all three by Friday." Then ask one question: "Is there anything you saw on site that you would want us to address that we have not discussed?" That question invites the specialist to tell you now what would otherwise appear for the first time in the credit committee report.

Monthly thread: personal brand

A personal brand, in this course, is the reputation that arrives in a room before you do. DFI teams talk to each other, to other lenders and to the authorities. A sponsor who answered honestly about a weakness and then closed it on time becomes known as someone whose action plans can be trusted, and his next appraisal is shorter.

The opposite reputation also travels. One appraisal in which a sponsor blamed his contractor can follow him for years. Ask yourself, Mr Shabazz, what a DFI specialist should say about you to a colleague, and whether your records would support it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is promising actions in the room that you cannot fund, which then become covenants you breach. The control is to bring a priced draft action plan to the appraisal, with owners and dates, and agree new items only after checking cost.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner prepares for the appraisal as if it were a sales meeting, with brochures and renderings. It is an audit. Bring logs, audits, surveys and signed reports.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and "I'll confirm by Friday." The appraisal uses the same discipline. Acknowledge the gap, bridge to the record, answer with a dated action, and confirm the cost before you commit.

Recap

The appraisal tests whether you run a system: across subcontractors, with records, owned by named people. Lead with the system, show the record, name the gap with a dated fix, and never blame the contractor or deny complaints. Promise only what you have priced, because it becomes a covenant.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on SPVs, recourse, security and sizing.
checklist: I can describe the workforce, including subcontractor workers, with numbers.
Every subcontract carries the same labour and safety clauses as the main contract.
I keep one incident and near-miss log with investigations and corrective actions.
I have a working grievance mechanism with logged, acknowledged and closed complaints.
I bring a priced draft action plan, with owners and dates, to the appraisal.
A named director signs the environmental and social report.
I never blame the contractor for a standard the lender holds me to.
I name my weakest area and propose a dated fix before I am asked.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a development finance institution's appraisal team asks about workers, safety and neighbours, it is testing whether I run a system, not whether I mean well. The question behind the question is whether I know the answer, whether the obligation reaches the subcontractors, and whether there is a record. So I lead with the system: how many workers, who employs them, the clauses every subcontract carries and the monthly payroll audit. Then the record: the incident log and investigations. Then the community: how a complaint is received, logged and closed. Then I name my weakest area and propose a dated, priced fix. I never say it is the contractor's problem, never say we have had no complaints, and never promise an action I have not priced, because every item in the action plan becomes a covenant. When the specialist writes, I stop talking. A named director, not a consultant, signs the report.
terms: Appraisal — a lender's detailed review of a project before approval, including site visits and interviews, written up for its credit committee.
Grievance mechanism — a documented process through which workers or neighbours can raise complaints and receive a response.
Environmental and social action plan — a dated list of actions a project must take to meet a lender's standards, usually attached to the loan as a covenant.

hostile.q: Your subcontractors' workers are not your employees. Why should we hold you responsible for how they are paid and housed?
hostile.a: Because you lend to my project, and the standard applies across the site, so I hold myself responsible. In practice that means every subcontract carries the same labour, safety and accommodation clauses as the main contract, our construction manager audits a sample of subcontractor payroll each month, and a breach is a default under the subcontract. Here is the last audit, including the two findings we raised and how they were closed.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 42 Review: SPVs, Recourse, Security and the Coverage Covenant
summary: Six questions test the week: the special purpose vehicle, the recourse spectrum, development finance institutions, the security package, sizing a project loan backward and the appraisal. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical term sheet, and a two-minute boardroom drill, make it stick.
body:
This week came down to one idea: in project finance the lender lends to the project's cash flow inside its own company, and it takes control of that company's money and contracts in exchange for not reaching yours.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a DFI specialist's question about workers?

A. Whether the sponsor knows the answer, whether the obligation reaches the subcontractors, and whether there is a record that proves it.

Q. What is a cost-overrun guarantee?

A. A guarantor's promise to fund construction costs above the budget, usually up to a cap and until completion, so the loan stays in balance.

Q. What is a conditional purchase agreement for land?

A. A binding contract to buy land that becomes unconditional only when stated conditions, such as financing, approvals or diligence, are met or waived by the deadline.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, project finance vocabulary sounds technical, but each term marks a place where control passes from you to someone else. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can read a project finance term sheet and know where the control sits. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is a special purpose vehicle, and what makes the ring-fence real?

Answer: A company formed to own one project and do nothing else, so its risks are separated from its owners. The ring-fence is real only if the SPV has its own accounts, books, minute book and decisions, and never commingles money with the sponsor.

Question 2. Describe the usual shape of recourse in a project loan.

Answer: Full sponsor support during construction, such as completion and overrun guarantees, released when a defined completion test is met, after which the loan is non-recourse except for carve-outs for bad acts.

Question 3. What does a development finance institution bring, and what does it require?

Answer: Longer tenor and the ability to bring commercial lenders alongside it, sometimes with concessional money. It requires the project to meet environmental and social standards, written into the loan as an action plan and covenants.

Question 4. Why does a lender want a pledge over the SPV's shares, not just a mortgage?

Answer: So that on enforcement it can take the company itself, keeping permits, contracts and licences intact, and sell a running business rather than a building stripped of its contracts.

Question 5. How do you size a project loan from the coverage covenant?

Answer: Divide NOI by the minimum coverage ratio to get maximum debt service; divide by the annuity factor to get the loan; compare with loan to cost and take the smaller; then add the reserve to uses before sizing equity.

Question 6. What is Rule 42?

Answer: The ring-fence protects the project from its owners, not from its own counterparties; before financial close, test every key counterparty's strength as if the project's survival depended on it, and have a replacement plan you can fund.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical term sheet extract and find the defects before reading on.

Project Loan Term Sheet, extract. Borrower: the SPV. Amount: 30,000,000 dollars, being 60 percent of project cost. Recourse: non-recourse to the Sponsor in all circumstances. Sizing: the Loan shall be sized at 60 percent of cost. Debt service coverage: minimum 1.30 on projected NOI of 4,000,000 dollars, 8 percent, 15-year level amortisation. Reserve: none required. Security: first mortgage over the Property. Distributions: permitted quarterly at the Sponsor's discretion. Environmental and social: the Borrower will comply with applicable law.

The defects. First, the arithmetic does not close: at 8 percent over 15 years, coverage of 1.30 on 4,000,000 dollars of NOI supports only about 26,340,000 dollars, so a 30,000,000 dollar loan breaches the covenant on day one. Second, sizing ignores the coverage test and states loan to cost alone. Third, "non-recourse in all circumstances" is not credible from a project lender; expect completion support and carve-outs, and a sponsor who relies on this line will be surprised by the final documents. Fourth, no debt service reserve and freely permitted distributions leave nothing between a bad quarter and a default. Fifth, security is a mortgage only, with no share pledge, account security or contract assignment, so the lender could not step in. Sixth, "comply with applicable law" falls short of a DFI's standards and suggests the action plan has not been discussed. A term sheet this generous is either a draft that will change, or a lender who has not done the work.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks: "Why does this loan come with so many documents, and what happens to us if it goes wrong?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "The project sits in its own company, and the lender lends to that company against the building's future cash flow, not against our other assets. During construction we support completion and overruns up to a cap. Once the building is finished and covering its debt service for a set period, that support falls away, and the loan becomes non-recourse except for carve-outs for bad acts. In exchange, the lender controls the project's money: revenue flows in a fixed order through accounts it holds security over, a reserve holds six months of payments, and distributions stop if coverage weakens. It takes security over the land, the company's shares, the accounts and the contracts, and signs direct agreements so it can step in rather than let the project die. The loan is sized on income, so coverage, not cost, sets the amount. If it goes wrong after completion, we lose our equity, not everything else we own."

Notice what the model answer leaves out: the names of the documents. An investor does not need to hear about accounts agreements and novation. The investor needs to hear where the money goes, who controls it and what the worst case costs. Translate the vocabulary into consequences, and keep the vocabulary for the lawyer.

Score your answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you explain recourse as a stage-by-stage shape, not a yes or no? Did you name the controls and why they exist? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing a structure protects you more than it does: a ring-fence that is not kept, a non-recourse label with carve-outs you have not read, a contractor whose strength you assumed. The control is to read the recourse provisions, the cure periods and your counterparties' accounts before close.

The beginner's mistake

Learning the words without the arithmetic. SPV, recourse and step-in are easy to say. The coverage calculation is what tells you whether the loan you are negotiating exists.

Callback

In Week 37, Priya taught the capital stack and the intercreditor agreement: who gets paid first and what the junior lender may do. Project finance adds the order of payments inside the project's own accounts, so that every dollar of revenue has a place in the queue before you see any of it.

Recap

The SPV ring-fences the project. Recourse is full during construction and limited after completion. DFIs lend long with standards attached. The security package and direct agreements let the lender step in. Coverage usually sizes the loan. Rule 42 makes you test your counterparties before close.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, project finance. The project sits in a special purpose vehicle that owns that project and nothing else, and the lender lends to it against the project's own cash flow. Recourse is a shape, not a switch: full support during construction, released at a completion test, and non-recourse after that except for carve-outs. Development finance institutions lend longer but write environmental and social standards into the loan. Because the lender cannot reach my other assets, it takes security over the land, the company's shares, the accounts and the contracts, and signs direct agreements so it can step in. The loan is usually sized on income: net operating income over the coverage ratio gives the payment, and the payment over the annuity factor gives the loan. Carillion taught Rule 42: the ring-fence protects the project from its owners, not from its own counterparties, so I test every key counterparty's strength before close.
terms: Ring-fence — the legal and practical separation of a project's assets and risks from its owners'.
Completion test — the defined conditions, physical and financial, that must be met before a sponsor's construction support is released.
Order of payments — the fixed sequence in which project revenue pays operating costs, debt service, reserves and only then distributions.

hostile.q: Your term sheet says non-recourse in all circumstances. Is that what you are telling your investors?
hostile.a: No. That line is from a draft, and I expect the final documents to require completion and overrun support during construction and carve-outs for bad acts throughout. I tell investors that after completion our loss on this project is limited to our equity, except for carve-outs we control by behaving properly, and I show them the carve-out list. I would rather understate the protection now than explain a surprise later.
